MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r1.claim: Mujahid says the mu'sirat are winds.

MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p719#4/r2.claim: Mujahid says thajjaj means poured out or flowing down.

MUQATIL:78:11-16/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:78:11-16/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:78:11-16/r4.claim: The clouds yield copious, successive rain: winds draw water from the lowest heaven's sea of provisions, raise and join clouds, and release rain with the wind; the Hour cannot come while any water remains.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r1.claim: Qatada says the mu'sirat are the sky, while some identify them as the wind.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p342#4/r2.claim: Qatada glosses thajjaj as pouring or flowing abundantly.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r2.claim: One explanation likens clouds to young women nearing menstruation; a muʿṣir is a girl nearing that age.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r3.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r3.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p508#9/r3.claim: Another explanation describes them as possessing spiraling winds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the muʿṣirāt are winds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r10.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r10.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r10.claim: Qatāda likewise says water is sent down from the heavens.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r11.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r11.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r11.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers rain-bearing clouds: the text says water comes “from” the muʿṣirāt, whereas winds contain no water and carry rain; clouds are the usual source of rain, even if sky is possible.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r2.claim: ʿIkrima's reading with bi- rather than min identifies the muʿṣirāt as winds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r3.claim: Mujāhid says the muʿṣirāt are winds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r4.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r4.claim: Qatāda says one reading has bi-l-maʿṣirāt, meaning the winds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r5.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the muʿṣirāt as winds and cites the verse about winds raising clouds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r6.speaker: سفيان
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r6.claim: Sufyān interprets the muʿṣirāt as clouds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r7.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās likewise identifies them as clouds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r8.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r8.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says the muʿṣirāt are clouds.

TAB-FULL:v24p12/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r9.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v24p12/r9.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the water descends from the sky.

TAB-FULL:v24p15/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r1.claim: Thajj means water pouring in a continuous succession, like the pouring of sacrificial blood.

TAB-FULL:v24p15/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ gloss thajj as pouring; Sufyān says it comes successively.

TAB-FULL:v24p15/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r3.speaker: ابن وهب
TAB-FULL:v24p15/r3.claim: Ibn Zayd says thajj means abundant, but al-Ṭabarī rejects this as unattested for quantity in Arabic and prefers continuous pouring, supported by the Prophetic phrase “the best Hajj is loud invocation and sacrifice.”

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3394#3/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3394#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3394#3/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the rain-bearing clouds as winds and the abundant water as pouring down.

NAHHAS:v5p125/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p125/r12.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p125/r12.claim: Exegetes say al-muʿṣirāt are winds or clouds; Abu Jaʿfar prefers clouds because the verse says 'from' them, not 'by' them.

NAHHAS:v5p125/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p125/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود
NAHHAS:v5p125/r13.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says God sends winds that collect water and drive it into clouds until they fill like a milch camel.

NAHHAS:v5p125/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p125/r14.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p125/r14.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says thajjājan means pouring down.

NAHHAS:v5p125/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p125/r15.speaker: ابن زيد
NAHHAS:v5p125/r15.claim: Ibn Zayd says thajjājan means abundant.

NAHHAS:v5p125/r16.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p125/r16.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p125/r16.claim: Abu Jaʿfar favors the common Arabic sense of pouring repeatedly; a hadith defines al-ʿajj as loud talbiyah and al-thajj as pouring sacrificial blood.

THALABI:v10p114/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p114/r1.claim: God sends wind that carries water, which gathers and descends in scattered drops like water drawn from a pregnant she-camel.

THALABI:v10p114/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r10.speaker: ابن زيد
THALABI:v10p114/r10.claim: Ibn Zayd says the rain is plentiful.

THALABI:v10p114/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r2.speaker: المؤرخ
THALABI:v10p114/r2.claim: Al-Mu'arrikh defines muʿṣirat as clouds with whirlwinds.

THALABI:v10p114/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r3.speaker: أبو العالية والربيع والضحاك
THALABI:v10p114/r3.claim: They say muʿṣirat are rain-bearing clouds before rain, compared to a woman approaching menstruation; Ibn Abbas transmits the same view.

THALABI:v10p114/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p114/r4.claim: Abu al-Najm's line supports the image of a woman whose time of menstruation is near.

THALABI:v10p114/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r5.speaker: المبرد
THALABI:v10p114/r5.claim: Al-Mubarrad interprets muʿṣirat as rain-bearing or pouring clouds.

THALABI:v10p114/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r6.speaker: ابن كيسان
THALABI:v10p114/r6.claim: Ibn Kaysan says muʿṣirat means sources of relief, derived from the verb used for pressing or yielding produce.

THALABI:v10p114/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r7.speaker: أبي بن كعب والحسن وسعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل بن حيان
THALABI:v10p114/r7.claim: These authorities interpret muʿṣirat as the heavens.

THALABI:v10p114/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p114/r8.claim: Thajjaj means pouring or flowing water.

THALABI:v10p114/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p114/r9.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v10p114/r9.claim: Mujahid glosses thajjaj as abundant rain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r1.speaker: مجاهد ومقاتل وقتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r1.claim: They understand al-muʿṣirat as winds; on this interpretation min functions like bi, so the rain came by means of the winds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r10.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r10.claim: He says clouds are called muʿṣirat because they squeeze out water.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r11.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r11.claim: The word can also describe grain ready to be cut, by analogy with rain ready to fall and be pressed from the clouds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r12.speaker: المبرد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r12.claim: On the cloud interpretation, the clouds retain water; ʿaṣr also refers to a refuge or shelter.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r13.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r13.speaker: المازني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r13.claim: A cloud is said to have made an iʿṣar when a strong dust whirlwind rises; this permits clouds with whirlwinds as the meaning.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r14.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r14.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r14.claim: He prefers clouds because whirlwinds are not rain-bearing winds, whereas the verse describes the muʿṣirat as bringing abundant water.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r2.speaker: عطاء ومقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r2.claim: They describe the al-muʿṣirat as a wind that brings rain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r4.claim: An al-muʿṣir cloud is laden with rain and ready to release it, like a young woman near menstruation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r5.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r5.claim: He says Arabic authorities disagree with al-Farra's definition of an adolescent girl as muʿṣir.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r6.speaker: أبو عبيد عن أصحابه
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r6.claim: A girl is called muʿṣir once she reaches maturity; a cited line says her period has approached.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r7.speaker: الكسائي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r7.claim: He defines a muʿṣir girl as one approaching twenty.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r8.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r8.claim: He says muʿṣir means the moment a girl menstruates, deriving the word from her confinement in a private room; ʿaṣr also means a place of refuge.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r9.speaker: غير الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p119/r9.claim: They explain the cloud term by analogy to a girl whose menstrual flow is released; iʿtaṣarat describes reaching that state.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:78:8-20/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:78:8-20/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:78:8-20/r4.claim: The “pressing clouds” are clouds that pour abundant water.

JISHUMI:v10p7243/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7243/r6.speaker: عكرمة
JISHUMI:v10p7243/r6.claim: He reports the preposition bi- in place of min- in “from the muʿṣirāt,” analogizing a Qur'anic phrase about angels descending on the Night of Decree.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r10.speaker: الأزهري
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r10.claim: Al-Azhari calls them cyclonic winds and explains من as ‘by’: the winds draw rain.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r11.speaker: أبو العالية والربيع والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r11.claim: They identify المعصرات as clouds; al-Walibi transmits this from Ibn Abbas.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r12.speaker: الفراء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r12.claim: Al-Farra says clouds ready to release rain resemble a young woman nearing menstruation before it begins.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r13.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r13.speaker: ابن كيسان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r13.claim: Ibn Kaysan derives the term from a verse about receiving rain and pressing fruit.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r14.speaker: الحسن وسعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل بن حيان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r14.claim: They interpret المعصرات as the heavens.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r9.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة ومقاتل والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p309#3/r9.claim: They identify المعصرات as winds that compress clouds; al-Awfi also transmits this from Ibn Abbas.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو العالية والربيع والضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r10.claim: The majority view takes المعصرات as rain-bearing clouds, named from squeezing out water; Ubayd Allah al-Anbari explains Hassan's verse this way.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r11.claim: Some identify المعصرات with water-filled clouds ready to rain, like a woman nearing but not yet having menstruated.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r12.speaker: ابن الكيسان
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r12.claim: Ibn al-Kaysan says clouds are called المعصرات because they bring relief, linking the word with 12:49.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r13.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r13.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada interpret المعصرات as winds that squeeze clouds; the reading بالمعصرات supports this view.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r14.speaker: ابن الزبير وابن عباس والفضل بن عباس وقتادة وعكرمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r14.claim: These readers have وأنزلنا بالمعصرات, a variant supporting the interpretation as winds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r15.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r15.claim: ثجاج means pouring rapidly and forcefully, like blood from a slaughtered animal.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r16.speaker: النبي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r16.claim: Asked about the best pilgrimage, the Prophet answered العج والثج, meaning fervent loud prayer and sacrificing the offering.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r9.speaker: الحسن وأبي بن كعب وابن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل وقتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p424#2/r9.claim: One interpretation of المعصرات is the heavens.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r15.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والكلبي
TABRISI:78:2-16/r15.claim: They interpret the “mu'sirat” as winds carrying cyclones; al-Azhari says min can mean bi because wind draws out rain.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r16.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r16.speaker: الربيع وأبي العالية
TABRISI:78:2-16/r16.claim: Another reading takes the mu'sirat as rain-bearing clouds; this is also transmitted by al-Walibi from Ibn Abbas.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r17.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r17.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:78:2-16/r17.claim: Thajjaj means rain pouring forcefully, or abundant rain.

TABRISI:78:2-16/r18.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:78:2-16/r18.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:78:2-16/r18.claim: Qatada explains thajjaj as rain falling in successive, continuous waves.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r1.speaker: أبي بن كعب والحسن وابن جبير
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r1.claim: One interpretation of al-muʿṣirāt is the heavens.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، عكرمة، قتادة، مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r2.claim: Another interpretation is the winds; Zayd ibn Aslam specifies the south wind, and min is understood as bi because the winds draw out rain.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r3.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r3.claim: He identifies the winds as the south wind.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r4.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r4.claim: Alternatively, the term means rain-bearing clouds, likened to a young woman nearing menstruation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r5.claim: He likewise compares the clouds to maidens who have nearly, but not yet, menstruated.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#2/r6.claim: Clouds are called muʿṣirāt when they are ready to rain, by analogy with crops described as ready to be harvested.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r1.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r1.claim: Thajjāj means abundant rain pouring down continuously.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p6#3/r2.claim: Thajja means to pour or stream.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r1.claim: Thajj can be intransitive, meaning to flow, or transitive, meaning to pour; the hadith pairs loud talbiya with pouring sacrificial blood.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas was called thajjaj because he poured forth abundant speech in his sermons.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r3.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل وقتادة
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r3.claim: Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qatada explain thajjaj as water flowing in a continuous, abundant stream.

RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r4.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p9/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses thajjaj as pouring, as though the water pours itself; the point is repeated rain and abundant benefit.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r10.claim: Qurtubi prefers clouds, since rain is known to come from them; if rain came from winds, wind would be the more natural source.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r7.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة وابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r7.claim: They explain mu‘sirat as winds that compress the clouds, while a second report from Ibn Abbas says it means clouds themselves.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r8.speaker: سفيان والربيع وأبو العالية والضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r8.claim: They say mu‘sirat are clouds ready to pour rain but not yet raining, like a young woman close to menstruation.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r9.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:78:11-14/r9.claim: Qatada also identifies mu‘sirat as the sky; al-Nahhas says these explanations can converge because winds pollinate clouds and bring rain.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r1.claim: The term mu‘sir can also mean a girl nearing puberty or a cloud nearly ready to rain; linguistic explanations connect both to approaching maturity or holding water.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r2.speaker: المبرد
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad says a mu‘sir cloud holds water and releases it little by little; related words can mean a refuge.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ikrima read “bi-l-mu‘sirat,” whereas the written codices have “min al-mu‘sirat.”

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r4.speaker: أبي بن كعب والحسن وابن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل بن حيان
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r4.claim: These authorities take “from the mu‘sirat” to mean from the heavens.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r5.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r5.claim: They explain thajjaj as pouring continuously and heavily; the word can be transitive or intransitive.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r6.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses thajjaj as pouring, with the water understood as pouring itself.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r7.claim: Asked about accepted pilgrimage, the Prophet answered: raising the voice in talbiya and spilling blood through sacrifice.

QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r8.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:78:14-15/r8.claim: Ibn Zayd says thajjaj means abundant; Qurtubi says this is the same meaning.

BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r1.claim: المعصرات may be clouds nearly pressed by winds, winds ready to squeeze clouds, or whirlwind-bearing winds; they initiate rain by forming or driving clouds, supported by reading بالمعصرات.

BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:78:14-16/r2.claim: ثجاجا means pouring abundantly; a Prophetic saying glosses الحج العج والثج as loud talbiya and flowing sacrificial blood, and the reading ثجاجا and مثاجج denote outflows.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#13/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#13/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p310#13/r1.claim: Al-muʿṣirāt may be clouds close to being squeezed by winds into rain, or the winds that form clouds and draw their moisture; a report says winds carry water from the sky to clouds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p381/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p381/r3.speaker: الفراء، ابن قتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p381/r3.claim: They explain المعصرات as rain-bearing clouds, like a girl near menstruation who has not yet menstruated.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r1.speaker: أبو النجم العجلي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r1.claim: His poem uses أعصرت for a young woman nearly at menstruation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r2.speaker: ثعلب، الأزهري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p382/r2.claim: ثج means forceful pouring; ثجاج describes heavy rain, and the verb can be transitive or intransitive.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، أبو العالية، الربيع، الضحاك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r1.claim: They take المعصرات as rain-bearing clouds, named from squeezing out water; another view says clouds containing water before rain.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r2.speaker: ابن كيسان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r2.claim: He derives المعصرات from succor, comparing وفيه يعصرون.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r3.claim: They identify them as winds that squeeze clouds, with rain attributed to its cause.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r4.speaker: ابن الزبير، ابن عباس، الفضل بن عباس، عبد الله بن يزيد، عكرمة، قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r4.claim: They read بالمعصرات with ب instead of من; Ibn Atiyya says this favors the wind interpretation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r5.claim: He allows the meaning winds ready to squeeze clouds or the clouds themselves.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384#2/r6.claim: ثجاجا means copiously pouring; its root also describes loud talbiya and pouring sacrificial blood. Al-Araj reads ثجاحا with ح.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384/r9.speaker: أبي، الحسن، ابن جبير، زيد بن أسلم، قتادة، مقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p384/r9.claim: They interpret المعصرات as the heavens.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r1.claim: Thajj means pouring in great quantity and force; the verb may be intransitive (‘the water poured’) or transitive (‘I poured it’).

SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r2.claim: A hadith phrase pairs ‘ajj’ and ‘thajj’: ‘ajj’ is raising one’s voice in the talbiya and ‘thajj’ is spilling sacrificial blood.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r3.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r3.claim: The cited poem uses ‘thajjajan’ for a copious, forceful flow, witnessing the sense of abundant pouring.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r4.speaker: الأعرج
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r4.claim: Al-A‘raj reads ‘thajjahan’ with a final unpointed ḥā’ instead of jīm.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:78:14#2/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the spillways of water ‘mathajih’ and uses ‘yantajihu’ for water flowing into the valley.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r1.claim: The preposition min may mark the starting point, while the reading with ba by Abd Allah ibn Yazid, ‘Ikrima, and Qatada introduces a causal sense; the readings reflect different meanings of ‘mu‘sirat’.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r10.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r10.claim: Al-Zamakhshari resolves the form issue by taking the hamza as entry into a state: clouds have entered the point at which they are about to bring relief through rain.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r2.claim: One interpretation is clouds nearing the point when winds press them to rain, like crops nearing harvest or a girl nearing puberty; Abu al-Najm’s line witnesses the usage ‘a‘sarat’.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r3.speaker: ابن قتيبة
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r3.claim: Ibn Qutayba cites Abu al-Najm’s verse ‘qad a‘sarat’ as evidence for the usage meaning that the time for a girl’s puberty is near.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r4.claim: Without the ‘nearing’ interpretation of ‘a‘sarat’, the form ‘mu‘sirat’ would be expected with a fatḥa on ṣād as a passive participle, since winds press clouds.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r5.claim: For ‘bil-mu‘sirat’, al-Zamakhshari allows winds ready to press clouds or clouds themselves, since water descends through them, analogous to giving from or by one’s hand.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r6.speaker: مجاهد
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r6.claim: Mujahid interprets ‘mu‘sirat’ as winds carrying whirlwinds.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r7.speaker: الحسن، قتادة
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r7.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret the word as the heavens: water passes from heaven to clouds, as though the heavens are pressing or enabling the pressing.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r8.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r8.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the min-plus-winds interpretation by saying winds form clouds and release their moisture, and reports that God sends winds carrying water from heaven if that report is sound.

SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r9.speaker: ابن كيسان
SAMIN-DURR:78:14/r9.claim: Ibn Kaysan proposes ‘mu‘sirat’ as ‘those bringing relief’, but the author questions how a form-IV participle can carry the meaning of the triliteral ‘aṣara’ (to relieve).

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r1.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Rabi‘ say “pouring” means water cascading down; al-Thawri says continuous and Ibn Zayd says abundant.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r2.claim: Ibn Jarir says thajj is not used in Arabic to mean mere abundance but means consecutive pouring; he cites the Prophetic phrase “the best pilgrimage is calling aloud and pouring,” referring to sacrificial blood.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303#2/r3.claim: A report about a woman with prolonged bleeding using thajj supports its sense of repeated, abundant flow.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r1.claim: Al-Awfi reports Ibn Abbas interpreting “the rain-bearing” as the wind; Ibn Abi Hatim also transmits this from Ibn Abbas through Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, and several early authorities agree that winds draw rain from clouds.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas also says the phrase means clouds; Ikrima, Abu al-Aliya, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, al-Rabi‘, and al-Thawri agree, and Ibn Jarir prefers this view.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r3.speaker: الفراء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r3.claim: Al-Farra’ defines them as clouds ready to release rain but not yet raining, comparing the word to a woman nearing menstruation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r4.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada reportedly interpret the phrase as the heavens; Ibn Kathir calls this an unusual view.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p303/r5.claim: The clearest interpretation is clouds, supported by the verse saying rain emerges from within clouds.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r11.claim: The sky, earth, rain, and plants resemble a reproductive pair: sky is male, earth female, water semen, and vegetation their offspring; springs and pools are implied.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.speaker: مقاتل
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r12.claim: Muqātil says every sign just mentioned is more astonishing than resurrection.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r4.claim: The muʿṣirāt are clouds heavy with water and close to being driven by winds into rain, which cools the sun’s heat and enables food and drink.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r5.speaker: الفراء
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r5.claim: Al-Farrāʾ defines a muʿṣir cloud as one that has gathered rain but does not yet rain, comparing it to a girl nearing menstruation without having begun.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r6.speaker: الرازي
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r6.claim: Al-Rāzī understands muʿṣirāt as clouds approaching rainfall, like a woman approaching menstruation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p297/r7.claim: Thajjāj describes abundant water pouring in successive streams; both the transitive and reflexive forms are used for pouring.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r1.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r1.claim: An unattributed poem describes black clouds whose water is thajjāj, providing poetic evidence for abundant, pouring rain.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-muʿṣirāt are winds and thajjāj is pouring water.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r3.claim: Ibn Masud describes clouds carrying water and raining it like a full udder, in heavy showers distributed by winds.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r4.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r4.claim: Ikrima identifies al-muʿṣirāt as clouds and thajjāj as pouring or abundant.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r5.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r5.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas says al-muʿṣirāt means from heaven and thajjāj means pouring.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r6.claim: The report notes the wording in Fadl ibn Abbas's codex for the rain verse.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r7.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r7.claim: Qatada reports Ibn Abbas's reading identifying the source as winds.

DURR-FULL:v8p392/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r8.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p392/r8.claim: Mujahid says al-muʿṣirāt are winds, reads bi-l-muʿṣirāt, and glosses thajjāj as pouring.

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r1.claim: The plural “We” signals the majesty and collectivity of the Divine Essence, Names, and Attributes.

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r2.claim: Muʿṣirāt are clouds the winds are about to squeeze into rain; the imminence prefix means they are ready, not that the rain has already fallen.

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r3.claim: The same imminence prefix appears in harvest-ready crops and a girl reaching puberty, supporting the sense “nearing the time.”

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r4.claim: Muʿṣirāt may alternatively mean winds about to squeeze out rain; the causative reading is unsuitable because the winds themselves are the squeezers.

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r5.claim: Thajjaj means abundant, successive flowing; the related hadith explains the pilgrimage’s loud talbiya and the pouring of sacrificial blood, while al-Zajjaj glosses it as pouring.

BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p229#2/r6.claim: There is no conflict with rain being sent from the sky: it may descend through clouds, or arise through celestial causes such as the sun lifting water from earth and seas into clouds.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو العالية والربيع والضحاك
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r1.claim: They understand المعصرات as clouds; the word can derive from a verb whose hamza marks the approach of their time to release rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r10.speaker: الأعرج
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r10.claim: Al-Aʿraj has a variant of ثجاجا, and the word مثاجح names places where water flows together.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r2.speaker: أبو النجم العجلي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r2.claim: Abu al-Najm's line about a maiden supports أعصرت for a young woman nearing menstruation, illustrating the time-nearing sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r3.speaker: ابن كسيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r3.claim: Ibn Kaysan derives the clouds' name from their giving aid and rain, as though rain were extracted from them by squeezing.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r4.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r4.claim: They also explain المعصرات as winds, which compress the clouds until they rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r5.speaker: المازني
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r5.claim: Al-Mazini takes them as clouds possessing cyclonic winds, which necessarily bring rain.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r6.speaker: ابن الزبير وابن عباس والفضل وعبد الله بن يزيد وعكرمة وقتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r6.claim: They read بالمعصرات with a causal or instrumental yāʾ, supporting the interpretation as winds; on that reading some construe من as causal, while others understand it as origin.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r7.speaker: أبو الحسن وابن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل وقتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r7.claim: They say المعصرات are the heavens; the author objects that the heavens are not squeezed to produce rain, and calls the proposed reconciliation far-fetched.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r8.claim: ثجاجا means pouring abundantly; the author prefers the intransitive sense because it is more common, though al-Zajjaj takes it transitively.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p10/r9.claim: A hadith describes the best pilgrimage as loud talbiya and the pouring of sacrificial blood; the objection that clouds could only yield a little water is dismissed as a relative comparison.

ELMALILI:78:14-30/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:78:14-30/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:78:14-30/r1.claim: Thajjaj describes abundant water or liquid pouring and rushing, whether intransitively or as something poured.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r1.claim: The surah has five attested names: al-Naba, Amma yatasa'alun, Amma, al-Tasa'ul, and al-Mu'asirat; al-Itqan lists four. It is Meccan and was placed after al-Ma'arij and before al-Nazi'at in Jabir ibn Zayd's revelation order.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r4.claim: Medinan, Syrian, and Basran counters count forty verses; Meccan and Kufan counters count forty-one.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p5/r5.claim: The surah rebukes mockery of the Quran and resurrection, proves resurrection through creation and humanity's first creation, warns of punishment, and contrasts believers' reward.

TABATABAI:78:13-14/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:78:13-14/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:78:13-14/r7.claim: The Qummi commentary glosses al-muʿṣirāt as clouds and thajjāj as successive pouring.

TABATABAI:78:9-16/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r10.claim: Al-muʿṣirāt are rain clouds, while thajjāj means water pouring abundantly.

TABATABAI:78:9-16/r11.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r11.speaker: قيل
TABATABAI:78:9-16/r11.claim: Some identify al-muʿṣirāt as winds that compress clouds to produce rain; on this reading min should mean bi.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r1.claim: Paired with al-Mursalat, this surah uses divine providence in the heavens and earth to establish Judgment as the necessary end of a purposeful world, rewarding the God-fearing and punishing rebels.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r2.claim: The surahs share an affirmative-question style aimed at deniers; each verse reproaches them while believers' glad tidings are understood against the warning.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p132/r4.claim: The signs of providence, mercy, wisdom, and power throughout earth and heavens show that humanity is not unchecked or unaccountable; its fixed day of reckoning must arrive.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r3.claim: Al-muʿṣirāt describes water-laden clouds or clouds producing rain, with no essential difference between these senses.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p142/r4.claim: Māʾ thajjāj means pounding, widespread, continuous rain; rain displays sky–earth harmony and supports monotheism, providence, and accountability.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:78:12/r1.claim: The seven firm heavens, sun, rain-bearing clouds, and life-sustaining growth display God's power to create a new realm, the afterlife.

STUDYQURAN:78:14/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:78:14/r1.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:78:14/r1.claim: Some read muʿṣirāt as the winds that bring rain clouds.

STUDYQURAN:78:14/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:78:14/r2.speaker: a small minority
STUDYQURAN:78:14/r2.claim: A small minority reads muʿṣirāt as referring to the heavens.
